text:
Solve this question and explain all key methods used 

Let a,b,c>0 satisfy abc=1. Find the minimum value of

\frac{1}{a^2-a+1}+\frac{1}{b^2-b+1}+\frac{1}{c^2-c+1}.

Try solving it first; send your steps and I’ll check them.

Given: a,b,c>0, abc=1, S(a,b,c)=1/(a^2-a+1)+1/(b^2-b+1)+1/(c^2-c+1)
Find: Determine whether S has a minimum, and find its infimum.

1. State the expression, domain, and constraint
   S(a,b,c)=(1)/(a²-a+1)+(1)/(b²-b+1)+(1)/(c²-c+1), a,b,c>0, abc=1
   We study the symmetric expression S over positive real numbers satisfying abc=1. Because a,b,c>0, the relevant denominators will be positive.

2. Establish positivity of the denominators
   a²-a+1= (a-frac 12 )²+frac 34>0
   The completed-square identity shows that a^2-a+1 is strictly positive for every real a. The same argument applies to b and c, so all reciprocals in S are well-defined and positive.

3. Compare each denominator with a simpler positive denominator
   a²-a+1<a²+1 (a>0)
   Since a>0, subtracting a from a^2+1 makes the quantity strictly smaller. The analogous inequalities hold for b and c.

4. Reverse the inequality after taking reciprocals
   frac 1a²-a+1>frac 1a²+1, frac 1b²-b+1>frac 1b²+1, frac 1c²-c+1>frac 1c²+1
   For positive denominators, a smaller denominator gives a larger reciprocal. Therefore each term of S is strictly larger than the corresponding term with denominator a^2+1, b^2+1, or c^2+1.

5. Reduce the problem to an auxiliary inequality
   x=a², y=b², z=c²
   Set x=a^2, y=b^2, and z=c^2. Since a,b,c>0, we have x,y,z>0. Moreover, the constraint abc=1 gives xyz=(abc)^2=1.

6. Prove the reciprocal-sum inequality under xyz=1
   (frac 11+x+frac 11+y+frac 11+z )-1=(1+x+y+z)/((1+x)(1+y)(1+z))
   Using xyz=1, combine the three fractions over the common denominator (1+x)(1+y)(1+z). The numerator of the difference from 1 simplifies to 1+x+y+z.

7. Conclude the auxiliary lower bound and its strictness
   frac 11+x+frac 11+y+frac 11+z=1+(1+x+y+z)/((1+x)(1+y)(1+z))>1
   Every quantity in the numerator and denominator is positive, so the fraction added to 1 is strictly positive. Hence the auxiliary sum is not merely at least 1; it is strictly greater than 1 for positive x,y,z with xyz=1.

8. Apply the auxiliary inequality to a,b,c
   frac 1a²+1+frac 1b²+1+frac 1c²+1 is not intended; instead frac 11+a²+frac 11+b²+frac 11+c²>1
   Applying Step 7 with x=a^2, y=b^2, and z=c^2 gives the required bound for the simpler reciprocal sum.

9. Obtain a strict lower bound for the original expression
   S(a,b,c)>frac 11+a²+frac 11+b²+frac 11+c²>1
   The first strict inequality comes from the termwise reciprocal comparisons in Step 4. The second comes from Step 8. Therefore S is strictly greater than 1 for every admissible triple.

10. Construct a family approaching the lower bound
   a=b=t, c=t⁻², t>0
   This choice satisfies the constraint because abc=t\cdot t\cdot t^{-2}=1. It provides admissible triples whose values can be studied as t becomes arbitrarily large.

11. Evaluate the expression along the family
   S(t,t,t⁻²)=(2)/(t²-t+1)+frac 1t⁻⁴-t⁻²+1
   Substitute a=b=t and c=t^{-2} into S. The first two terms are equal, while c^2-c+1=t^{-4}-t^{-2}+1.

12. Take the limit and distinguish infimum from minimum
   lim ₜ→∞S(t,t,t⁻²)=lim ₜ→∞ ((2)/(t²-t+1)+frac 1t⁻⁴-t⁻²+1 )=1
   The first term tends to 0 because its denominator grows without bound, while the second term tends to 1 because t^{-4} and t^{-2} tend to 0. Thus values of S can be made arbitrarily close to 1 from above. Since Step 9 proves S>1 for every admissible triple, no triple attains 1. Therefore 1 is the infimum, but a minimum does not exist.

13. Final conclusion
   boxed ∈fₐ,b,c>₀, ₐbc=₁ (frac 1a²-a+1+frac 1b²-b+1+frac 1c²-c+1 )=1, but no minimum is attained.
   The expression is always strictly greater than 1, yet admissible values approach 1 arbitrarily closely. Hence the requested minimum does not exist; the rigorous lower-bound value is the infimum 1.

Answer: boxed ∈fₐ,b,c>₀, ₐbc=₁ (frac 1a²-a+1+frac 1b²-b+1+frac 1c²-c+1 )=1, nexists min .
For every positive a,b,c with abc=1, we have a^2-a+1<a^2+1 and therefore 1/(a^2-a+1)>1/(a^2+1), with analogous inequalities for b and c. Setting x=a^2, y=b^2, z=c^2 gives xyz=1 and 1/(1+x)+1/(1+y)+1/(1+z)>1. Thus S>1 always. The family a=b=t, c=t^{-2} satisfies abc=1 and gives S=2/(t^2-t+1)+1/(t^{-4}-t^{-2}+1)→1 as t→∞. Therefore 1 is the infimum, but it is never attained, so no minimum exists.

operations.title: The constrained expression
operations.caption: S(a,b,c)=\frac{1}{a^2-a+1}+\frac{1}{b^2-b+1}+\frac{1}{c^2-c+1},\qquad a,b,c>0,\qquad abc=1
operations.narration: We study S over positive a, b, and c with product one. The proof has two parts: show S is always above one, then construct values that approach one.

operations.title: Positive denominators
operations.caption: a^2-a+1=\left(a-\frac12\right)^2+\frac34>0
operations.narration: Before comparing fractions, we must know their denominators are positive. Completing the square makes that immediate.

operations.title: A smaller denominator
operations.caption: a^2-a+1<a^2+1\quad(a>0)
operations.narration: Because a is positive, subtracting a from a squared plus one makes the denominator smaller. The same comparison will hold for b and c.

operations.title: Reciprocals reverse
operations.caption: \frac1{a^2-a+1}>\frac1{a^2+1},\qquad \frac1{b^2-b+1}>\frac1{b^2+1},\qquad \frac1{c^2-c+1}>\frac1{c^2+1}
operations.narration: For positive quantities, a smaller denominator produces a larger reciprocal. Applying this term by term gives three strict inequalities.

operations.title: A useful substitution
operations.caption: x=a^2,\qquad y=b^2,\qquad z=c^2,\qquad xyz=(abc)^2=1
operations.narration: The comparison has reduced the problem to denominators of the form one plus a square. Rename those squares x, y, and z. The product constraint becomes xyz=1.

operations.title: Subtracting one
operations.caption: \left(\frac1{1+x}+\frac1{1+y}+\frac1{1+z}\right)-1=\frac{1+x+y+z}{(1+x)(1+y)(1+z)}
operations.narration: Consider the reciprocal sum for x, y, and z. Combining the fractions over a common denominator reveals the amount by which the sum exceeds one.

operations.title: The auxiliary sum exceeds one
operations.caption: \frac1{1+x}+\frac1{1+y}+\frac1{1+z}=1+\frac{1+x+y+z}{(1+x)(1+y)(1+z)}>1
operations.narration: Here x, y, and z are positive. Therefore the displayed remainder is positive, and the reciprocal sum is strictly greater than one.

operations.title: Return to a, b, c
operations.caption: \frac1{1+a^2}+\frac1{1+b^2}+\frac1{1+c^2}>1
operations.narration: Substituting back the squares of a, b, and c gives a strict lower bound for the simpler sum.

operations.title: A strict global bound
operations.caption: S>\frac1{1+a^2}+\frac1{1+b^2}+\frac1{1+c^2}>1
operations.narration: The original expression is strictly larger than the simpler reciprocal sum, and that simpler sum is strictly larger than one. Thus S is always strictly above one.

operations.title: An escaping family
operations.caption: a=b=t,\qquad c=t^{-2},\qquad t>0,\qquad abc=1
operations.narration: To test whether one is the true lower boundary, choose a=b=t and c=t to the power minus two. The product remains exactly one.

operations.title: Evaluate along the family
operations.caption: S(t,t,t^{-2})=\frac{2}{t^2-t+1}+\frac{1}{t^{-4}-t^{-2}+1}
operations.narration: Substitution gives two identical contributions from a and b, while the c-term becomes the expression involving negative powers of t.

operations.title: Approaching the boundary
operations.caption: \lim_{t\to\infty}S(t,t,t^{-2})=\lim_{t\to\infty}\left(\frac{2}{t^2-t+1}+\frac{1}{t^{-4}-t^{-2}+1}\right)=1
operations.narration: As t tends to infinity, the denominator of the first term grows, so that term vanishes. The negative powers in the second denominator vanish, leaving one. The values therefore approach one.

operations.title: Infimum, not minimum
operations.caption: S>1\ \text{for every admissible }(a,b,c),\qquad S(t,t,t^{-2})\to1^+
operations.narration: We have proved S is greater than one for every admissible triple, so one is never attained. But the family gets arbitrarily close to one. Therefore one is the infimum, while no minimum exists.

operations.title: FINAL ANSWER
operations.caption: \boxed{\inf_{a,b,c>0,\,abc=1}\left(\frac1{a^2-a+1}+\frac1{b^2-b+1}+\frac1{c^2-c+1}\right)=1,\qquad \nexists\min}
operations.narration: The expression has infimum one over positive a, b, and c with abc equal to one. Since every value is strictly greater than one, no minimum exists.
